title: A Bell for the Hymn
premise: Gideon Halloran hosts a small-town overnight radio show, and for twenty years the calls have come from listeners who died days earlier—voices he has quietly recorded, rationalized, and never told anyone about. When his new sleep-monitoring equipment captures a second voice in his own bedroom answering questions he never asked aloud, Gideon learns the dead are being counted, and when the count reaches a number only the voice knows, the town of Hymn's Ferry will be collected. To save his estranged family and the living remnants of the town, Gideon must finally break his silence, expose what he knows, and offer himself as a substitute entry in the count. In the end, the bell of the old hymn church rings once for every soul spared—and once more, unanswered, for him.
about_author: Silas Whitlock is the pen name of a former late-night radio engineer who spent a decade working the graveyard shift at stations across the rural Northeast, collecting the strange calls and dead air that fuel his fiction. He writes horror about small towns, old frequencies, and the things that answer when no one is broadcasting.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. During his 2 a.m. broadcast, a caller named Marcy requests a hymn; Gideon recognizes her voice and later confirms she died six days ago. He archives the call with practiced calm, but his hands shake. The beat is dread disguised as routine—the reader learns the secret before anyone else does.

chapters.title: The Archive Under the Floor
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. We tour his basement archive: two hundred cassettes of calls from the dead, meticulously labeled over twenty years. His rules are laid out—never answer personal questions, never say their names twice, never tell anyone. A tape from 2004 ends mid-sentence with a sound like a bell. Emotional beat: guilt wearing the mask of order.

chapters.title: Hymn's Ferry Counts Its Dead
chapters.summary: Deputy Ruth Okonkwo's POV. A missing-persons report on Marcy exposes how many residents have vanished or died this season—eleven in three months, far above normal. Ruth notices the obituaries all mention hearing bells. She begins her own list. Beat: institutional skepticism cracking into unease.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. New sleep-recording software meant to catch his sleep-talking instead captures a low second voice in his darkened bedroom answering questions he never asked aloud: 'How many are left?' 'Seven.' Gideon plays it back forty times. Beat: the watcher realizes he is watched.

chapters.title: Questions You Shouldn't Ask
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, intercut with the recordings. Against his own rules, Gideon asks the voice questions during waking hours and records the answers: the count, the collection, the bell that rings for each soul claimed. The voice knows his childhood nickname. Beat: curiosity curdling into terror as the answers get personal.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Stopped Calling
chapters.summary: Naomi Halloran's POV, in the city. Gideon's estranged sister gets a voicemail from their mother—who died last spring—asking Naomi to 'come home before the counting.' Naomi, unaware of anything supernatural, books a trip partly out of grief, partly to confront Gideon about Mom's funeral he skipped. Beat: love complicated by resentment.

chapters.title: Eleven Bells at St. Ambrose
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. The derelict hymn church rings eleven times at 3:11 a.m.; Ruth investigates and finds fresh rope-burn on the bell pull and eleven names scratched into the oak door—Marcy's among them, dated the day after her death. Beat: evidence without explanation, justice instinct ignited.

chapters.title: Family Arrives
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Naomi arrives unannounced with her teenage son Theo, intending to stay a week. Gideon tries to hide the archive and the recordings; Theo, a tinkerer, finds the sleep-capture rig and hears the second voice within an hour. Beat: the walls of secrecy failing exactly when family needs protecting most.

chapters.title: What the Voice Wants
chapters.summary: Gideon and Theo's shared POV via alternating scenes. They test the voice: it lies about small things, tells truth about large ones. It says the count stands at seven and that 'the host who listens' may be added or subtracted. Gideon realizes his twenty years of listening made him part of the mechanism. Beat: complicity revealed.

chapters.title: The List in the Door
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth cross-references the scratched names against cold cases going back decades—all unsolved deaths, all injustices the law never answered. Her theory: something in Hymn's Ferry collects those whose deaths went unmourned or unavenged. She drives to the station to confront the night host everyone whispers about. Beat: justice outside the law takes shape.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Station
chapters.summary: Dual POV, Gideon and Ruth. Ruth lays out her evidence; Gideon, cornered, plays her one cassette. Ruth's worldview breaks and rebuilds in a single scene. They form an uneasy alliance: she'll help evacuate the seven remaining names if Gideon helps her understand the count. Beat: isolation ending, trust beginning.

chapters.title: Six
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The church rings six times; one of the seven named townsfolk dies peacefully in his sleep, smiling. The voice on the recording sounds satisfied. Gideon understands the count isn't random—it's descending toward a final number, and the last name on the list is his own. Beat: fatalism setting in.

chapters.title: Rules of the Count
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo deciphers patterns in the archive: the voice only counts souls 'owed'—deaths wronged, covered up, or forgotten. A death acknowledged and mourned seems to close an account. The family tests it by holding a proper memorial for Marcy; the next morning her name on the church door is crossed out. Beat: hope through ritual and truth-telling.

chapters.title: The Town That Wouldn't Listen
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Attempting to warn and gather the remaining families, Ruth meets denial, hostility, and one chilling exception: old Mrs. Vane, who has known about the count since 1968 and has been leaving offerings at the church for fifty years. She explains the bell was built to ring the count down, not up. Beat: lore deepens, deadline sharpens.

chapters.title: Naomi's Voicemail
chapters.summary: Naomi's POV. Their mother's voice calls Naomi directly now, begging forgiveness for a family secret: their father's death years ago was ruled accidental but wasn't—an unpaid debt that started the Hallorans' entry in the count. Naomi must decide whether to tell Gideon the truth that will break him. Beat: loyalty versus truth made flesh.

chapters.title: The Truth About Dad
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Naomi confesses: their father was killed covering for someone powerful, and the family took hush money and silence. Gideon's twenty years of listening weren't chance—the count has been calling him home to settle it. Rage, grief, and clarity arrive together. Beat: the personal wound becomes the key.

chapters.title: Four Left, One Night
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. With four names remaining, the group works through the night holding improvised memorials, forcing the town to hear the truths behind each owed death. Two accounts close; the church bell tolls erratically, angry. The voice on the recordings stops answering questions and starts asking them. Beat: desperate momentum, victory with a price.

chapters.title: The Name That Won't Close
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Their father's account won't close—mourning isn't enough because the wrong was never named publicly. The only way to settle it is confession on air, naming the still-living man responsible. Doing so means lawsuits, danger, and destroying what's left of the family's reputation. Beat: the cost of truth made explicit.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. On live radio, Gideon confesses everything: the calls from the dead, the archive, his father's murder, the name of the man who ordered it. The town listens; the guilty man's house lights snap on; the church bell begins to toll—not four times, but continuously, counting down through the small hours. Beat: climax of exposure, courage at maximum cost.

chapters.title: The Collection
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. At 3:11 a.m., the count reaches its final number and the collection comes anyway—for the one debt no memorial can pay: Gideon's own, the listener who stayed silent for twenty years while the dead called for help. He walks to the church willingly, trading himself to close the ledger. Beat: sacrifice, terror transfigured into purpose.

chapters.title: One Bell More
chapters.summary: Naomi and Ruth's POV. Dawn. The bell rings once for every soul spared, then once more with no name attached—a bell for Gideon. The archive tapes play static where his voice used to be, except one: a final recording of Gideon saying goodbye, telling Naomi to keep the station running. Beat: grief and awe braided together.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, one year later. Theo runs the overnight show now, playing hymns and taking ordinary calls from the living. Sometimes, at 3:11, a familiar warmth fills the studio and the request line clicks open though no one dials. He always says thank you on air. Final beat: belonging found in inheritance, the dead at rest, the bell silent—but ready.
